t: The pre-Christian religion of Scandinavia worshipped gods such as Odin, Thor, Freyr and Freyja, with sacrifices, feasts and rituals led by chieftains and kings, in a world of nine realms around the world tree Yggdrasil.

Its myths, of a world made from the body of a giant and destroyed at Ragnarök, are known mainly from Icelandic texts written down by Christians in the 13th century, two centuries after the conversion.
Displaced by Christianity between the 10th and 12th centuries, it gave English four of its weekday names and a mythology that has inspired art and literature from Wagner to Tolkien and modern film.
dyk: A soapstone mould found in Denmark, from the 10th century, was made to cast both Christian crosses and the hammers of Thor, so that a smith could sell to customers of either faith.
ev: The Viking raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne opens the Viking Age
King Harald Bluetooth raises the Jelling stone, recording that he made the Danes Christian
The Icelandic assembly, the Althing, adopts Christianity, allowing pagan worship in private for a time
Adam of Bremen describes the temple at Uppsala with images of Thor, Odin and Freyr
Snorri Sturluson writes the Prose Edda, a handbook of Norse myth and poetry
The Codex Regius, the manuscript of the Poetic Edda, is written in Iceland
Iceland recognises the modern Ásatrú fellowship as a religion

f.origin: Scandinavia, from the religion of the Germanic peoples of the Iron Age; best known from the Viking Age, about 800 to 1100
f.founder: None: it was led by chieftains, kings and seeresses, without a founder or a priestly order
f.scriptures: No scripture: its myths survive in skaldic poems, the Poetic Edda and Snorri Sturluson’s Prose Edda, written down by Christians in 13th-century Iceland
f.followers: None as an ancient tradition: Scandinavia was Christian by the 12th century; a modern revival, Ásatrú, was recognised in Iceland in 1973
